name: Red yeast rice

lead: Red yeast rice is rice fermented with Monascus mold, used for centuries in Chinese food and medicine and now sold for cholesterol. It appears in longevity routines as part of keeping the heart and body healthy over decades.

It contains monacolin K, identical to lovastatin, which inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that makes cholesterol. Randomized trials report lower LDL cholesterol, and a large Chinese trial of the extract Xuezhikang in post-heart-attack patients reported fewer coronary events. It has not been studied for appearance outcomes.

paras: Taken as a daily oral supplement, usually as part of a cholesterol or longevity routine, often as an alternative some people consider alongside diet changes.

Reported effects resemble statins, including muscle and liver problems. Monacolin content varies and some products contain citrinin; EFSA in 2018 found no safe intake for monacolin preparations, and the FDA treats products with substantial monacolin K as drugs.

angle.text: Red yeast rice is taken for cholesterol and appears in longevity routines as part of keeping the body healthy over decades. Its cholesterol effect has been studied in trials; it is not used for a direct appearance outcome.

lead: Red yeast rice is rice fermented with the mold Monascus purpureus. It has long been used in Chinese cooking and traditional medicine and is now sold as a supplement for cholesterol [1][2]. It contains monacolins, including monacolin K, which is chemically identical to the drug lovastatin [2][3].

In appearance and healthy-aging circles it is discussed as a route to better cardiovascular and metabolic health, the kind of foundation that supports energy, training capacity and long-term vitality. The chain is indirect: lower LDL cholesterol, healthier vessels, more years of active life. Randomized trials report lower LDL cholesterol [4][5][6], and a large Chinese trial of the extract Xuezhikang in post-heart-attack patients reported fewer coronary events [7].
Safety and quality questions are a recurring part of the discussion, including variable monacolin content, possible citrinin contamination and statin-like muscle and liver effects [2][8][9].

paras: Red yeast rice, also called red koji rice, hong qu or angkak, is made by growing Monascus purpureus on steamed rice for several days at room temperature. The grains turn red at the core and reddish-purple outside, and the finished product is sold as dried grain, a cooked paste or a powder [2]. China is the largest producer [2].

The koji tradition of molded grains is described as dating to about 300 BCE, and Wikipedia reports documented Chinese use of red yeast rice from at least the first century CE [2]. In kitchens it colors and flavors dishes such as char siu, Peking duck, red rice vinegar, fermented tofu and Fujian red wine chicken, and it colors rice wines including huangjiu and Japanese akaisake; in the Philippines, angkak colors and preserves fermented fish, shrimp and rice dishes [1][2].

In traditional Chinese medicine red yeast rice has been used for improving circulation, resolving stasis and aiding digestion [1][2]. Wikipedia notes that the Ben Cao Gang Mu (c. 1590) recommends it for the body, digestion and blood circulation [2]; Grokipedia describes medicinal use from around 800 CE [1].

Modern supplements are sold for lowering LDL and total cholesterol. A 2021 JACC seminar describes red yeast rice extracts as among the most effective cholesterol-lowering nutraceuticals, with monacolin K acting as a weak, reversible inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase [10]. Reviewers suggest it is a possible option for mild to moderate hypercholesterolemia in lower-risk people who cannot or prefer not to take statins [10][11].

In longevity-minded communities it is mentioned alongside other cardiovascular supplements as part of keeping blood lipids in range over the long term. No published study has examined it for skin, body composition or other appearance outcomes.

The mold produces a family of polyketide metabolites called monacolins, along with fatty acids and trace elements [3]. Monacolin K is identical to lovastatin, which was isolated from Aspergillus in the late 1970s and became the prescription drug Mevacor; researchers in the United States and Japan identified monacolins in Monascus in the same period [2][3]. Wikipedia reports that a properly processed Went-strain powder is about 0.4 percent monacolins, roughly half of it monacolin K [2].

Like statins, monacolin K blocks HMG-CoA reductase, a rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis in the liver, which lowers circulating LDL [2][10]. The mold also yields other compounds, collectively reviewed in a 2013 paper on Monascus secondary metabolites [8].

A 12-week double-blind randomized trial in 83 US adults tested a proprietary Chinese red yeast rice supplement alongside an American Heart Association-style diet [4]. A 2006 meta-analysis of randomized trials examined it for primary hyperlipidemia [5], and a 2015 meta-analysis reported significant LDL reduction while noting that safety was uncertain [6]. A 2009 randomized trial studied statin-intolerant patients [12].

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 double-blind trials lasting 4 to 24 weeks reported a mean absolute reduction of about 36 mg/dL in LDL cholesterol and 37 mg/dL in total cholesterol, without significant change in HDL or triglycerides, and judged side effects neither frequent nor threatening [13]. A narrative review reports LDL reductions of roughly 15 to 34 percent versus placebo, similar to low-dose first-generation statins, at about 3 mg per day of monacolin K [14]. The 2019 and 2021 reviews cite 15 to 25 percent LDL reduction within 6 to 8 weeks, with similar drops in apolipoprotein B and C-reactive protein [10][11].

In a 2023 single-blind trial that randomized 190 adults to low-dose rosuvastatin, placebo or one of six supplements including red yeast rice, the percent LDL reduction with rosuvastatin was greater than with any supplement or placebo over 28 days [9].

Monacolin content varies widely between products and is rarely labeled; a 2010 analysis of commercial products found markedly different monacolin levels [15], and Wikipedia reports a range from 0.31 to 11.15 mg per 600 mg capsule in an analysis of 12 US products [2]. Some products contain citrinin, a fungal compound toxic to the kidney [2].

Myopathy and liver injury have been reported, mirroring statin effects [2][16]. A 2011 review estimates that 10 to 15 percent of statin users develop muscle symptoms, which is the context for monacolin-related reports [16]. EFSA concluded in 2018 that no safe intake could be established for monacolin-containing preparations, noting severe reactions at doses as low as 3 mg per day [2]. Wikipedia advises against use in pregnancy and breastfeeding [2].

In March 2024 Japanese authorities ordered recalls of Kobayashi Pharmaceutical benikoji products after reports of kidney illness and deaths; the company found puberulic acid in recalled lots, and the cause was under investigation. Hospitalizations exceeded 100 and five deaths were reported by late March 2024, and Kobayashi discontinued the products that August [2].

The FDA moved against the product Cholestin in 1998, an appeals court ruled for the agency in 2001, and the agency issued warning letters in 2007 and advised consumers not to buy products that may contain an unauthorized drug [2]. Products containing monacolin K are regulated as drugs, while products with negligible monacolins that make no cholesterol claims generally fall outside enforcement [2].

EFSA's 2018 opinion found no safe intake for monacolin preparations [2]. Grokipedia also mentions earlier European health-claim approvals for monacolin K and a citrinin limit, which differ from the later EFSA opinion [1].

Randomized trials report LDL-lowering with red yeast rice [4][5][6][12][13], and meta-analyses place the effect in the range of low-dose statins [13][14]. In the Chinese Coronary Secondary Prevention Study, nearly 5,000 patients with prior myocardial infarction took the extract Xuezhikang [7]; Wikipedia reports about 45 percent fewer heart attacks, 31 percent fewer cardiac deaths and 33 percent fewer deaths from any cause over roughly 4.5 years [2].

A Japanese multicenter trial tested a low-dose product in mild dyslipidemia, and a 2019 trial of Monascus pilosus and a Scandinavian trial of a product called HypoCol also reported lower cholesterol [17][18][19]. A 2023 trial tested a nattokinase-Monascus combination over four months [20]. Studies of red yeast rice for body fat, skin or appearance have not been published.
